units.title: Tidal Volume, Boyle's Law, Three Pressures, Intrapleural Negativity & Intra-Alveolar Pressure Changes
units.sec: Tidal Volume, Boyle's Law, Three Pressures, Intrapleural Negativity & Intra-Alveolar Pressure Changes
units.guide:
Pressures in respiratory physiology (p193): tidal volume is the air moving in and out of the lungs, normal 500 mL; Boyle's law gives tidal volume α 1/TPP. Three pressures are intrapleural, intra-alveolar (IAP) and transpulmonary (TPP = intra-alveolar/intrapulmonary − intrapleural).
Intrapleural pressure is the pressure in the pleura, which has lymphatics and a vacuum (lung collapses, chest expands); it is negative except in forceful expiration, where it becomes positive. Inspiration is active — respiratory muscles and diaphragm contract, the chest wall expands and pleural pressure falls; expiration is passive.
Intra-alveolar pressure is zero at rest, −1 mmHg in inspiration and +1 mmHg in expiration; the printed intrapleural trace runs from −2 to −3 mmHg at the start of inspiration to −7 to −8 mmHg at the end.

units.title: Transpulmonary Pressure Equations, TPP Trace Values, Intrapleural Fluid Cohesiveness, Pneumothorax Note & Static Compliance
units.sec: Transpulmonary Pressure Equations, TPP Trace Values, Intrapleural Fluid Cohesiveness, Pneumothorax Note & Static Compliance
units.guide:
Transpulmonary pressure (p194): total TPP = TPP of lung + TPP of chest wall; TPP of chest wall = intrapleural − atmospheric pressure; total TPP = IAP − atmospheric pressure. The trace is drawn around an atmospheric pressure of 760 mmHg, with intra-alveolar +1 mmHg in expiration and a TPP of 7–8 mmHg at end-inspiration.
Lungs are held to the thorax by intrapleural fluid cohesiveness (water molecules attracting one another and resisting being pulled apart) and by negative intrapleural pressure. In pneumothorax, intrapleural equals intrapulmonary pressure, TPP is 0 and the lung is not inflated.
Static compliance is 200 mL/cm H2O, maximal at mid-range pressure, and equals ΔV/ΔP with ΔP = TPP; at tidal volume it is the inflation of lung per unit change in pressure.

units.title: Hysteresis Loop, Surface Tension vs Elastic Recoil, Elastin/Collagen & Obstructive vs Restrictive Compliance Curves
units.sec: Hysteresis Loop, Surface Tension vs Elastic Recoil, Elastin/Collagen & Obstructive vs Restrictive Compliance Curves
units.guide:
Hysteresis (p195): the ΔV/ΔP curve differs between inspiration and expiration because inspiration occurs against resistance while expiration is passive and needs no extra force. The resistances are surface tension (more important, overcome by surfactant) and elastic recoil pressure of the lung, which arises from elastin (elastic force) and collagen (tensile strength).
Obstructive disease (COPD, emphysema): ↑ static compliance, curve shifted up and left, loss of elastin → ↓ ERP → easier to inflate. Restrictive disease (ILD): ↓ static compliance, curve shifted down and right, fibrosis → ↑ collagen → ↑ ERP → difficult to inflate.
The plotted curves are labelled high compliance (emphysema), normal, and low compliance (pulmonary fibrosis).

units.title: Dynamic Compliance (Only-Dynamic vs Static-and-Dynamic Falls) & Elastic Recoil Pressure of the Respiratory System at RV/FRC/TLC
units.sec: Dynamic Compliance (Only-Dynamic vs Static-and-Dynamic Falls) & Elastic Recoil Pressure of the Respiratory System at RV/FRC/TLC
units.guide:
Dynamic compliance (p196) equals static compliance plus resistance, and static and dynamic compliance move together. Foreign body, kink in the ET tube and intrathoracic obstruction lower only dynamic compliance, whereas pulmonary edema, consolidation, atelectasis and pneumothorax lower both.
ERP of the respiratory system: total ERP = ERP of lung + ERP of chest wall. At residual volume the chest wall alone contributes a negative, outward ERP and inflation is easy; at FRC (equilibrium/relaxation volume, RV + ERV) chest wall and lung together give zero ERP and inflation is easy; at TLC both forces act downwards giving a positive ERP and inflation is difficult. Residual volume is the air left after forceful expiration, normally 1.2 L.
